questions.stem: A sorting algorithm is stable when:
options: it uses no memory besides the array
it takes the same time on every input of size n
elements with equal keys keep their original relative order
it makes at most n - 1 swaps
questions.explanation: Stability is about equal keys and their arrival order. (a) is "in place"; (d) is a property of selection sort.

questions.stem: A sort is in place when:
options: it needs only O(1) extra memory besides the array it sorts
it returns the same list object it was given
questions.explanation: The course sorts return a new list, but they rearrange their working Array with O(1) extra slots — so they are in place in this sense. (b) is what Python's list.sort does; it is not the definition.

questions.stem: Which of these sorts is not stable, as written in the course?
options: merge sort that takes from the left half on a tie
questions.explanation: Its long-distance swap can jump an element over an equal one. Bubble and insertion sort move a value only past strictly greater ones; a merge that takes from the left on a tie is stable (Week 10).

questions.stem: Bubble sort, with the early exit, on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] makes how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: The first pass compares the 5 neighbour pairs, swaps nothing, and the early exit stops the sort: n - 1 = 5.

questions.stem: Selection sort on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] makes how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 = n(n-1)/2. Selection sort scans the whole rest in every round, sorted or not.

questions.stem: The array after the first pass of bubble sort on A is:
questions.explanation: The 9 is carried to the end; the pass swaps 5 and 2, then 9 and 1, 9 and 7, 9 and 3. (a) is the first round of selection sort; (c) is after the second pass.

questions.stem: The array after the first round of selection sort on A is:
questions.explanation: The minimum, 1 at index 3, is swapped with the 5 at index 0. (a) is bubble sort's first pass.

questions.stem: Insertion sort on A. The array after the round that inserts a[3] (the value 1) is:
questions.explanation: Before that round the prefix is [2, 5, 9]; the 1 shifts all three right and lands at index 0.

questions.stem: How many inversions does [3, 1, 2] have?
questions.explanation: (3, 1) and (3, 2). The pair (1, 2) is in order.

questions.stem: The number of shifts insertion sort makes is always equal to:
options: the number of inversions of the input
questions.explanation: Each shift moves current past one larger value before it — one inverted pair — and changes the order of no other pair (W9-E3).

questions.stem: The best case of insertion sort is:
questions.explanation: One comparison per round and no shifts: n - 1 comparisons.

questions.stem: Selection sort is the best of the three basic sorts when:
options: writing an element costs much more than comparing two
questions.explanation: At most n - 1 swaps, whatever the input. It is not stable (c), gains nothing from sorted input (a), and (d) is counting sort.

questions.stem: The largest number of swaps selection sort makes on 10 values is:
questions.explanation: At most one swap per round, and there are n - 1 rounds. 45 (b) is the number of comparisons.

questions.stem: counting_sort([4, 0, 4, 1]) makes a counts array of how many slots?
questions.explanation: k = max + 1 = 5: one counter for each value 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

questions.stem: Counting sort on n values from the range 0 .. k - 1 takes:
questions.explanation: One pass to count (n), one over the counters (k), n writes.

questions.stem: Counting sort is a bad choice when:
options: the range of the values is much larger than n
questions.explanation: Sorting two values up to a million needs a million counters and a loop over all of them.

questions.stem: In the worst case, every comparison sort of n values needs at least:
questions.explanation: A decision tree with at least n! leaves has height at least log2 n!, which is Θ(n log n).

questions.stem: The fewest comparisons that can sort any 4 values in the worst case, by comparing, is at least:
questions.explanation: 4! = 24 orders, and 24 = 16 < 24 ≤ 32 = 25: at least ⌈ log2 24 ⌉ = 5 comparisons in the worst case.

questions.stem: The decision-tree argument for the lower bound uses the fact that:
options: the tree needs at least n! leaves, and a binary tree of height h has at most 2h leaves
questions.explanation: Two different input orders must end at different leaves, and h yes/no answers can tell apart at most 2h cases.

questions.stem: A _steps generator yields its working list itself (not a copy) before each comparison. Then frames = list(generator) holds:
options: the final, sorted state in every frame
questions.explanation: Every frame holds a reference to the same list; by the time you look, it is sorted. step_slider hides the bug by copying each frame as it arrives; list(generator) does not.

questions.stem: A plain sort runs its _steps generator to the end, and the generator copies the array before each of its about n2/2 comparisons. The plain sort costs:
questions.explanation: n2/2 copies of n values each: Θ(n3). The reference fixes it with snapshot=_live in the plain sort (Lecture 09, "The price of watching").

questions.stem: Bubble sort on [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1] makes how many swaps?
questions.explanation: Reversed input has every pair inverted: 6 × 5 / 2 = 15 inversions, and bubble sort makes one swap per inversion.
